new_statements.quote: The rules for stress assignment can be laid out as follows: by default, the first syllable carries main stress. Closed syllables, however, attract stress. If there are closed syllables, the main stress moves to the last closed syllable, as long as it is not the final syllable of a word [...] Examples like ˈkam.ni.bak ‘friend’ show that the stress never moves to the final syllable, even when the syllable is heavy. Patterns where the final syllable is stressed are possible though, because prefixes are not part of the stress domain. In monosyllabic nouns that host a possessive prefix, the stress generally remains on the stem
new_statements.citation: Schackow, Diana. 2015. A grammar of Yakkha (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 7). Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.17169/langsci.b66.106.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.4 'Stress assignment', printed p. 57 (PDF p. 75); continuation pp. 58-61
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: is a symlink to pp., the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'A grammar of Yakkha', Author Diana Schackow, XeTeX 2015; text layer present, no scanned needed). I ran extracted text on PDF pp. 75-79 (= printed pp. 57-61, sec. 3.4 'Stress assignment'). The quoted passage is there verbatim: p. 57 'The rules for stress assignment can be laid out as follows: by default, the first syllable carries main stress. Closed syllables, however, attract stress. If there are closed syllables, the main stress moves to the last closed syllable, as long as it is not the final syllable of a word, demonstrated by the examples in Table 3.11..'; the reader's [..] spans Table 3.11 and exx. (10)-(11) on p. 58…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yakkha (Tumok dialect): main stress is word-initial by default; if the word contains closed (heavy) syllables, main stress falls on the rightmost closed syllable that is not word-final; the final syllable of the stress domain is never stressed even if heavy. Prefixes are outside the stress domain (so prefixed monosyllabic stems surface with final stress); clitics are outside it except the nominalizers =na/=ha, which count.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'It is hard to tell whether there is secondary stress. Even in words with five syllables.. no secondary stress could be detected.' Secondary stress is clearly audible in compounds (on the first syllable of the second member, main stress on the first syllable of the whole compound) and on the verbal stem in long inflected verb forms (p. 61).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexicalized monosyllabic kin terms with possessive prefix take initial stress (ˈa.mum 'grandmother'); compounds may override the ban on word-final stress; triplicated ideophonic adverbs (se.re.ˈreː 'drizzling') always have final stress with a lengthened final vowel; nominalizers =na/=ha are inside the stress domain unlike other clitics.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word minus prefixes; phrase-level clitics attach after stress is assigned. Statement describes the Tumok village variety of Yakkha, not a variety called 'Lambichhong' (the grammar never uses that name).
new_statements.identity_note: lamb1277 'Lambichhong' [lmh] is a Glottolog Bookkeeping (retired/spurious) entry: 'derives from a misinterpretation of the questionnaires used in the Linguistic Survey of Nepal 1981-1984 and should simply be filed under Yakkha' (van Driem 2001:682-683, as cited on the Glottolog page). Ethnologue 15 (2005) had it as a separate Eastern Kiranti language of 500 speakers in Muga/Pakhribas panchayats, Dhankuta district, 'sometimes incorrectly called Mugali or Yakkha'; ISO code lmh is still active. No description of any variety under the name Lambichhong exists. The quoted stress statement is for Yakkha (yakk1236), Tumok village dialect (Sankhuwasabha), from Schackow 2015, who explicitly has no data on the southern Dhankuta varieties (the area Ethnologue assigned to Lambichhong; cf. '?Mugali' under Greater Yakkha in Bickel 2008's tree reproduced as her Fig. 2.8). If the catalog keeps one entry per real language, this key should be merged into yakk1236 rather than given its own row; the same Schackow file is already

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Stress assignment' (printed pp. 57-61, PDF p. 75ff): default initial stress; closed syllables attract stress, main stress goes to the last closed syllable but never the word-final syllable; prefixes outside the stress domain; clitics do not affect stress except nominalizers =na/=ha; secondary stress only clearly in compounds and on verb stems; triplicated ideophonic adverbs have final stress. Describes the Tumok dialect; the book never mentions 'Lambichhong'.
Not used for stress; lists [lmh] Lambichhong as a 'duplicate code' under Yakkha.
